questions.question: What is cloud computing? Give the formal definition.
questions.answer: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute power, database storage, applications, and other IT resources through a cloud service platform with pay-as-you-go pricing. The two key terms are 'on-demand' (instant, no pre-ordering) and 'pay-as-you-go' (you pay only while using it).

questions.question: What are the five NIST characteristics of cloud computing?
questions.answer: 1. On-demand self-service — provision resources without human intervention from the provider. 2. Broad network access — access from any device over the network. 3. Resource pooling — multi-tenancy; multiple customers share physical infrastructure with logical isolation. 4. Rapid elasticity — automatically scale up and down based on demand. 5. Measured service — usage is metered and billed exactly per consumption.

questions.question: What are the six advantages of cloud computing?
questions.answer: 1. Trade CAPEX for OPEX — pay for usage instead of buying hardware. 2. Benefit from massive economies of scale — AWS's scale drives prices down. 3. Stop guessing capacity — scale elastically based on actual usage. 4. Increase speed and agility — resources in minutes, not weeks. 5. Stop spending money on data centers — focus on products. 6. Go global in minutes — deploy worldwide using AWS infrastructure.

questions.question: What is the difference between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS? Give an AWS example of each.
questions.answer: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) — provides raw compute, storage, and networking. Customer manages OS and above. AWS example: EC2. PaaS (Platform as a Service) — provider manages infrastructure; customer manages only app and data. AWS example: Elastic Beanstalk. SaaS (Software as a Service) — complete product managed by provider; customer just uses it. AWS example: Amazon Rekognition.

questions.question: What is an AWS Region and what is an Availability Zone?
questions.answer: A Region is a physical geographic location (like us-east-1 for N. Virginia) containing a cluster of AWS data centers. An Availability Zone is an isolated data center facility within a Region. Each Region has 3–6 AZs, physically separated to prevent disaster cascades, connected by high-bandwidth private networking. AZs are the foundation of high availability on AWS.

questions.question: What are the four factors for choosing an AWS Region?
questions.answer: Remember CLAP: Compliance — legal data residency requirements always come first. Latency — deploy close to your users. Availability — not all services exist in all regions, check before choosing. Pricing — costs vary by region; us-east-1 is typically cheapest.

questions.question: What is the AWS Shared Responsibility Model?
questions.answer: A framework defining security boundaries: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud — physical hardware, data centers, networking, hypervisor, and global infrastructure. The customer is responsible for security IN the cloud — data, IAM, OS configuration (on EC2), application security, and network/firewall configuration. The boundary shifts by service type: more customer responsibility with IaaS, less with managed services.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Private Cloud, Public Cloud, and Hybrid Cloud?
questions.answer: Private Cloud: used exclusively by one organization, not public-facing. Can be managed by a third party. High control, high cost. Public Cloud: AWS/Azure/Google Cloud — resources owned by provider, shared among customers, delivered over internet, pay-as-you-go. Hybrid Cloud: a mix of on-premises (or private cloud) and public cloud. Companies keep sensitive/regulated workloads on-premises while using public cloud for flexible workloads.

questions.question: What are AWS Global Services? Give three examples.
questions.answer: Global services are AWS services that are not scoped to a specific Region — they apply worldwide. When you access them in the console, it shows 'Global' instead of a region. Examples: IAM (Identity and Access Management), Amazon Route 53 (DNS), Amazon CloudFront (CDN), and AWS WAF.

questions.question: What is the AWS data transfer pricing rule for ingress vs egress?
questions.answer: Data transfer INTO AWS from the internet is always free (ingress). Data transfer OUT from AWS to the internet is charged (egress). This is a frequently tested CLF-C02 fact. Within AWS, cross-region transfers are charged; within the same AZ transfers are generally free.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to explain cloud computing to a non-technical stakeholder. How did you handle it?
questions.answer: (Situation) At my previous role, a department head was skeptical about cloud migration, worried about losing control of servers. (Task) I needed to explain the value of cloud without overwhelming technical jargon. (Action) I used the analogy of renting an apartment vs buying a house — with cloud (renting), you don't worry about maintenance, repairs, or paying for empty rooms. You pay only for what you use. I then walked through specific cost savings from eliminating idle server capacity. (Result) The stakeholder approved the migration pilot, which reduced infrastructure costs by 40%.

questions.question: Describe a scenario where you would recommend a Hybrid Cloud deployment instead of full public cloud.
questions.answer: (Situation) A healthcare client had patient records they legally could not move outside their country's borders, but they wanted cloud elasticity for their analytics and appointment scheduling systems. (Task) Design a deployment model that satisfies compliance without abandoning cloud benefits. (Action) Recommended Hybrid Cloud: sensitive patient data stays on on-premises servers within the country; the analytics platform and scheduling app deploy to AWS in the local region. AWS Direct Connect provides secure private connectivity between the environments. (Result) The client achieved compliance while gaining cloud scalability for their non-sensitive workloads — best of both models.

questions.question: A junior developer asks you why they can't see their EC2 instance after switching regions in the console. How do you explain it?
questions.answer: (Situation) A junior developer launched an EC2 instance in eu-west-1 (Ireland) and couldn't find it after switching the console to us-east-1 (N. Virginia). (Task) Explain AWS regional scoping. (Action) Explained that EC2 is a regional service — the instance physically lives in Ireland's data centers. Switching the console view to N. Virginia shows only resources in N. Virginia. Switched back to eu-west-1 together and the instance appeared. Also showed the region selector in the top-right corner and advised to always verify region before creating resources. (Result) The developer understood the regional model and adopted the habit of checking the region selector first.

questions.question: How would you respond to a client who says 'the cloud is less secure because multiple companies share the same hardware'?
questions.answer: (Situation) An enterprise client was concerned about multi-tenancy and data security when evaluating AWS migration. (Task) Address their concern about shared infrastructure. (Action) Explained that multi-tenancy uses hypervisor-level logical isolation — other customers cannot access your data or resources even on the same physical server. Additionally, AWS's physical data center security (biometric access, 24/7 surveillance, armed guards, strict compliance certifications) exceeds what most enterprises can implement themselves. AWS also undergoes independent third-party audits for ISO 27001, SOC 2, PCI DSS. (Result) Client agreed to proceed with a security assessment, which led to full migration approval.

questions.question: Your company's CTO says 'we save money by managing our own servers.' Under what conditions might this be true?
questions.answer: (Situation) The CTO believes on-premises is cheaper at their current scale. (Task) Analyze when on-premises actually is cost-competitive. (Action) Explained that on-premises can be cheaper when: workloads are highly predictable and run at near-100% capacity 24/7 (elastic scaling's cost advantage disappears), the company is at very large scale with dedicated hardware negotiation leverage, they have existing hardware investment not yet depreciated, and they have a large infrastructure team already. For variable or unpredictable workloads, new projects, and teams wanting agility, cloud wins. (Result) Agreed to analyze specific workloads — steady-state batch jobs stayed on-premises; new development and variable traffic services moved to AWS.

questions.question: A client asks who is responsible for patching their database. How do you answer if they use EC2 with MySQL vs Amazon RDS?
questions.answer: (Situation) A client had both EC2-hosted MySQL and RDS databases and was confused about patching responsibility. (Task) Explain the Shared Responsibility Model for each case. (Action) EC2 + MySQL = customer patches everything including the OS and MySQL engine — this is IaaS, you manage the software stack. Amazon RDS = AWS patches the database engine and OS automatically — this is a managed service (PaaS), AWS owns the infrastructure layer. Customer still manages database configuration, users, and access. Documented this as a responsibility matrix for their security team. (Result) The client established separate patching schedules: manual for EC2, policy-based monitoring for RDS.

questions.question: How would you explain Availability Zones to a business stakeholder who asks 'why do we need to pay for servers in multiple locations?'
questions.answer: (Situation) A business stakeholder was questioning the cost of multi-AZ deployment for their e-commerce site. (Task) Justify multi-AZ architecture in business terms. (Action) Asked: 'If your website went down for 4 hours on Black Friday because one data center had a power outage, how much would that cost?' Explained AZs as insurance — they're physically separated so a single disaster can't take down everything. Running across 3 AZs means one can fail completely and the site keeps running. The added cost is minimal compared to even one hour of downtime revenue loss. (Result) Stakeholder approved multi-AZ deployment as a business risk management decision.

questions.question: A team wants to develop and launch a new feature in 2 hours. In your previous company, this took 3 weeks due to server procurement. How did migrating to cloud solve this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Our on-premises process required hardware procurement, racking, OS installation, and configuration — 3 weeks minimum for new capacity. (Task) Eliminate this bottleneck after cloud migration. (Action) Post-migration to AWS: developers launch EC2 instances from the console in minutes. Infrastructure as Code (CloudFormation) templates mean full environments can be created in under 30 minutes. CI/CD pipelines deploy to new environments automatically. The 3-week blocker became a 30-minute self-service operation. (Result) Feature release cycle improved dramatically — teams could experiment cheaply and release faster. This matches the 'increased speed and agility' cloud advantage.

questions.question: How do you advise a client on region selection when they have users in both the USA and India?
questions.answer: (Situation) A SaaS company served users in both New York and Mumbai with an application hosted only in us-east-1. Mumbai users complained of 250ms latency. (Task) Improve global performance. (Action) Analyzed traffic split — 60% USA, 40% India. Recommended a multi-region strategy: primary deployment in us-east-1 for US users, secondary deployment in ap-south-1 (Mumbai) for India. Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing directs each user to the nearest region automatically. Also considered CloudFront Edge Locations for static content. (Result) Mumbai latency reduced to under 50ms. US users unaffected. Cost increased modestly but NPS improved significantly.

questions.question: An executive asks you to summarize in 30 seconds why the company should migrate to AWS. What do you say?
questions.answer: (Situation) 30-second elevator pitch for AWS migration to a time-pressed executive. (Task) Convey maximum value with minimal words. (Action) Said: 'Right now we're paying for servers whether we use them or not. With AWS, we only pay for what we actually use — like switching from a monthly parking spot to paying per hour. We can scale instantly during peak periods without buying hardware. We eliminate disaster risk by running across multiple data centers. And we can go from idea to deployed product in days instead of months.' (Result) Executive asked for a formal business case — the 30-second pitch opened the door for full migration planning.

questions.question: How does the Shared Responsibility Model differ between IaaS and managed services like RDS? Provide a detailed comparison.
questions.answer: The boundary shifts significantly: With IaaS (EC2): Customer manages OS patching, runtime installation, database installation, database patching, application code, security config, network rules. AWS manages physical hardware, hypervisor, and data center. With PaaS/Managed Services (RDS): Customer manages database users, access permissions, query performance, data, encryption choices, security group for DB access. AWS manages database engine patching, OS patching, automatic backups, multi-AZ failover infrastructure, hardware, hypervisor. The key insight: moving up the service model stack transfers infrastructure management to AWS, but data and access control always remain the customer's responsibility regardless of service type.

questions.question: Architect a fault-tolerant, highly available web application using the AWS Global Infrastructure concepts covered in this topic.
questions.answer: Using AWS Regional Infrastructure for HA: 1. Choose a Region with 3+ AZs (most regions qualify). 2. Deploy EC2 instances (web and app tiers) across all 3 AZs — failure in one AZ leaves 2/3 capacity available. 3. Use a multi-AZ RDS deployment — automatic failover to standby in another AZ. 4. Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that distributes traffic across all AZs and performs health checks — routes away from unhealthy AZs automatically. 5. Use Amazon CloudFront (Edge Locations) to cache static content globally — reduces latency for all users. 6. S3 for static assets — 11 nines of durability (replicated across AZs automatically). Result: The application can survive complete failure of one AZ with minimal user impact — the textbook AWS HA architecture.

questions.question: A company is deciding between full cloud, on-premises, and hybrid for their three workloads: (1) real-time fraud detection, (2) archival patient records with strict national regulations, (3) development/testing environments. How would you architect each?
questions.answer: Each workload needs different treatment: (1) Real-time fraud detection — Public Cloud (AWS). High variability, needs rapid scaling for transaction spikes, low latency via Edge Locations, benefits from AWS ML services (Fraud Detector). Cost: pay per transaction. (2) Archival patient records — Private Cloud or On-Premises. National data residency laws prevent cloud migration. If the country has an AWS Region, could use that Region with strict data governance — else remains on-premises. (3) Dev/Test environments — Public Cloud (AWS). No regulatory constraints, highly variable usage (burst during sprints, idle otherwise), pay-as-you-go eliminates waste. Overall architecture: Hybrid Cloud. On-premises/private for regulated data, AWS for scalable operational workloads, secure connection (AWS Direct Connect) between environments.

questions.question: Explain how CAPEX vs OPEX analysis would work for a company considering cloud migration, including when on-premises might still win.
questions.answer: CAPEX (On-premises) analysis: $2M server purchase + $300K/year depreciation + $500K/year staff + $200K/year power/cooling + $100K/year maintenance = $3.1M year 1, ~$1.1M ongoing. Servers run at 40% average utilization — 60% is wasted spend. OPEX (AWS) analysis: Pay only for actual usage. If average 40% utilization of equivalent resources = $440K/year. Elastic scaling means peak capacity only when needed. No staff for hardware maintenance. On-premises wins when: utilization is consistently near 100%, scale is massive (billions of requests/day), long-term stable workloads (Reserved Instances can reduce by 60%), existing depreciated hardware still has life. Recommendation: Hybrid economic model — steady, predictable workloads on-premises or Reserved Instances; variable/new workloads pay-as-you-go.

questions.question: A global media company is building a video streaming service that needs to serve users in 30 countries with less than 50ms latency. How would you use AWS Global Infrastructure?
questions.answer: Multi-layer global architecture: 1. Amazon CloudFront (400+ Edge Locations in 40+ countries) — caches video segments at Edge Locations worldwide. 95% of requests served from Edge Location nearest the user — typically under 50ms. 2. Origin servers in 3-4 AWS Regions — us-east-1 (Americas), eu-west-1 (Europe), ap-southeast-1 (Asia), ap-south-1 (India). Each region handles requests from its geographic zone. 3. S3 for video storage — store master files in S3; CloudFront pulls and caches segments. 4. Route 53 geolocation routing — directs users to the nearest regional origin if CloudFront cache misses. 5. Multi-AZ in each region — ensures regional availability even during AZ failures. Result: 30-country coverage from 4 Regions + CloudFront's global edge network, all without building physical infrastructure in 30 countries. This is 'go global in minutes' in practice.
